3.quote: From 2018, it could borrow only from the IBRD and through non-concessional IDA terms, both at higher interest rates, with transitional support during the IDA18 period (FY18–20) [3].
According to the World Bank, official financing alone will not be enough to meet these needs, so Vietnam will also have to borrow on capital markets and pay more to do so [3].

The World Bank's 2019 Performance and Learning Review records transitional IDA18 support of SDR 1.593 billion (approximately USD 2.3 billion before a subsequent allocation reduction), alongside continuing access to IBRD financing [3].

4.quote: In July 2026, the World Bank reclassified Vietnam as an upper-middle-income economy [4].

Vietnam's reclassification as an upper-middle-income economy in 2026 means that future World Bank borrowing will rely on IBRD terms [4].

33.quote: CCSEP, for instance, prepared an environmental and social impact assessment for each city and a resettlement policy framework for all four [33].
The sector's investment requirement was estimated at around USD 771 million per year, while expected funding covered only about 27% [33].

The borrower was the Government of Vietnam, the World Bank served as the financier, and implementation was decentralized to the four provinces of Quang Binh, Binh Dinh, Khanh Hoa and Ninh Thuan through Project Management Units (PMUs) under the direction of provincial People's Committees [33; 43].

Expected outcomes were measured by three main indicators: approximately 290,000 direct beneficiaries, 256,000 people gaining access to sanitation via household sewer connections, and a 100% service cost recovery level [33].
CCSEP was designed as an Investment Project Financing operation, financing specific investment items rather than policy reforms or results, as the other two instruments do [33, Data Sheet].

The IDA credit was denominated in SDR, with a 25-year maturity including a 5-year grace period, an interest rate of 2% per annum (0.75% service charge and 1.25% interest), a commitment fee of 0.5% per annum, and no front-end fee [33, para. 44].

The IDA credit was denominated in SDR, with a 25-year maturity including a 5-year grace period, an interest rate of 2% per annum (0.75% service charge and 1.25% interest), a commitment fee of 0.5% per annum, and no front-end fee [33, para. 44].

Component 1 (Sanitation Infrastructure Expansion, USD 140.7 million base cost) included flood control works, drainage and wastewater collection networks, wastewater treatment plants, school and public sanitation facilities, revolving funds for household connections, and solid waste management [33, para. 31].

Note: The table shows base costs only. The difference from the total project cost comes from contingencies (USD 37.9 million), VAT (USD 22.3 million), and capitalized fees and interest (USD 4.8 million), which are also financed by the three sources. Minor differences in totals are due to rounding in the PAD.
Phan Rang–Thap Cham received the largest share (USD 87.9 million), followed by Nha Trang (USD 72.0 million), Dong Hoi (USD 58.4 million) and Quy Nhon (USD 55.3 million) [33, Annex 2, Tables 2.2–2.5].
Each province opened a designated USD account at a commercial bank, with ceiling amounts adjusting based on three-month financial forecasts [33, Annex 3, para. 21].
Counterpart funding increased from USD 37.4 million to USD 50.0 million, raising its share from 13.7% to 20.8% [33, Annex 2; 43].

The financing agreement became effective on 18 January 2018, about five and a half months behind the original schedule of 3 August 2017, and the loan closing date had to be extended by 18 months, from 31 December 2022 to 30 June 2024 (Table 3.3.1.1) [33; 55; 43].
The project was classified as Category A for environmental and social safeguards, subject to the involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12 and procurement under World Bank guidelines [33].
The PAD estimated 1,486 affected households, of which 329 required relocation [33].
The goal was for each city to have a service management unit, and for the project to deliver 14 performance-based service contracts, 4 service tariff roadmaps and 4 connection policies [33].

The IBRD loan was only 16.8% of the planned cost (14.2% after adjustment) and fully financed Component 2, while the larger IDA credit financed the sanitation infrastructure [33, Annex 2, Table 2.1; 43].
As Table 3.3.3.1 shows, direct beneficiaries reached 64% of the target and sewer access only 38%, while cost recovery stood at 98% of the 100% target [33; 43].
Regarding climate resilience, the PAD set a target to reduce flood risks for approximately 44,000 people and to construct 17 km of embankments, 22 km of roads and 5 bridges [33].
TEP received USD 500 million with a 26-year maturity and a 10-year grace period [21], and CCSEP's IBRD loan carried a 29-year maturity [33].
In CCSEP, the loan became effective five and a half months late, and three disbursement conditions depended on approvals by the Ministry of Finance and provincial People's Committees [33].

The borrower was the Government of Vietnam, the World Bank served as the financier, and implementation was decentralized to the four provinces of Quang Binh, Binh Dinh, Khanh Hoa and Ninh Thuan through Project Management Units (PMUs) under the direction of provincial People's Committees [33; 43].

The reasons given were savings after the bidding process, changes in the source of payment for IBRD fees and interest as stipulated by the Government, and the depreciation of the SDR, while the project scope remained unchanged [43].
Counterpart funding increased from USD 37.4 million to USD 50.0 million, raising its share from 13.7% to 20.8% [33, Annex 2; 43].

The financing agreement became effective on 18 January 2018, about five and a half months behind the original schedule of 3 August 2017, and the loan closing date had to be extended by 18 months, from 31 December 2022 to 30 June 2024 (Table 3.3.1.1) [33; 55; 43].
Procurement, financial management and safeguards were all rated Moderately Satisfactory, and legal covenants were fully complied with [43].
In Phan Rang, the Phan Dang Luu resettlement site was completed, with 1,400 out of 1,586 compensation plans approved, while Dong Hoi and Quy Nhon largely completed their resettlement activities [43].

After the restructuring, the World Bank recommended adding qualified staff, improving coordination between PMUs and provincial departments, amending contract terms with contractors and consultants, increasing supervision frequency, and holding monthly progress meetings alongside biweekly site clearance meetings [43].

The IBRD loan was only 16.8% of the planned cost (14.2% after adjustment) and fully financed Component 2, while the larger IDA credit financed the sanitation infrastructure [33, Annex 2, Table 2.1; 43].
As Table 3.3.3.1 shows, direct beneficiaries reached 64% of the target and sewer access only 38%, while cost recovery stood at 98% of the 100% target [33; 43].

Each city established a PSMU; drainage and wastewater assets were handed over to local People's Committees; road assets were transferred to transport departments; household connection policies and septic tank sludge management plans were issued; and tariff roadmaps were approved [43].

Three direct causes lie behind these problems, as analyzed in Section 3.3.3: disagreements over land prices and compensation, which led one-third of the approved plans to be rejected; land-use restrictions imposed since 2016 without completed acquisition, which prolonged residents' waiting; and weak PMU capacity and coordination with provincial authorities, which delayed compensation and contract execution [43].
In CCSEP, the reforms under Decree No. 80/2014/ND-CP produced service management units, connection policies and tariff roadmaps, and cost recovery reached 98% [43].
CCSEP disbursed nothing in 2017 and 2018 and only about 36% of its loan capital by late 2022 [43].
